name: Omar Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build mobile apps for local councils at a company of about sixty people: bin day reminders, parking permits, reporting potholes. I start the day by asking my AI assistant to summarise overnight crash reports, then I fix the worst one before stand-up. I love when an older resident tells the council the app finally made sense. What drains me is council procurement, where one button change needs three meetings and a form.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does life outside work look for you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ines, who's a social worker, in a one-bed flat above a launderette. We're both on modest pay, and I send a bit each month to my dad, who runs a corner shop that's barely breaking even. So our savings are under a month, which is silly for someone who works in tech, but that's the truth of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd lose a few bets with my friends, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the tools are handy but they're not magic, and I've always said that. Online I'd probably post that the real story was always public money and who gets it. At work I'd say let's use what works and stop the hype slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be using it every day, because it saves me maybe an hour on boring code. The bigger worry for me is council budgets, because our contracts get cut whenever money's tight. If two councils don't renew in April, the company will shed people, and I'm not senior enough to be untouchable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant for crash summaries and tests and get faster at the boring bits. I'd start building a free volunteer rota app for the food bank Ines works with, partly to help and partly as a portfolio piece. I'd try to save one month's rent by summer, even if it means sending Dad a bit less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, but not relaxed. My job feels okay, but council money and Dad's shop are always in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your dad's shop in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, slowly squeezed by the supermarket that opened on the ring road. My dad doesn't need AI to struggle; his corner shop is doing that already. I'd probably help him set up online orders, which is the one useful thing I can actually do for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd send your dad less. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, for about ten minutes, then fine. He'd say he never asked for it, which is true. Mum would phone me afterwards to say thank you anyway.

say: I'd say AI tools are **handy but not magic**, which I've always said.
I'd say the real story is **public money** and who gets it, not the hype slides.
think: I'd still use AI daily because it saves me about **an hour** of boring code.
My real worry is **council budgets**, since lost contracts mean the company sheds people.
do: Keep using the **AI assistant** for crash summaries and tests, getting faster each month.
Build a free **rota app** for the food bank as a portfolio piece.
Save **one month's rent** by summer, even if Dad gets a little less.
feel: Settled but **not relaxed**, with **council money** and Dad's shop always in mind.
S0.quote: My dad doesn't need AI to struggle; his corner shop is doing that already.
fieldNote: He's a **daily AI user** who still sees the hype clearly, a mix not every adopter has.
His real exposure is **council contracts**, with money also flowing out to his dad.
The **food bank app** joins his values to a practical career move.

steps.text: Use the AI assistant for overnight crash summaries every morning
Build a free volunteer rota app for the food bank
Save one month's rent by summer by sending Dad less

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I think is most likely, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are powerful and the question is who they serve. I'd write a blog post on how councils could use AI to clear housing repair backlogs instead of cutting staff. At work I'd volunteer to run the team's AI training, because someone kind should do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm on the right side of this one, at least for a few years. I already use the tools all day, so I'd be the one they keep while they hire fewer juniors. That bothers me more than it reassures me, because some of those juniors would have been me five years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within the first month I'd set up AI code review and test-writing for the whole mobile team. I'd pitch the company on selling an AI version of our pothole app to councils, so we grow instead of shrink. I'd also join the tech workers' union branch and push for a rule that saved time goes into training, not cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly energised, with a guilty edge. I can see a path for me, and I can see people I like falling off it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about falling off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rachel, our tester, who's been here twelve years and checks every release by hand. AI testing is exactly the thing I'd be setting up. I'd want to bring her in on it, not replace her, but I don't control the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it odd to push automation and union rules at the same time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. Ines says the same about her job: the tech should take the paperwork so she can spend more time with families. I want the AI tools, and I want rules about who gets the time they save.

say: I'd say AI is powerful and the question is **who it serves**.
I'd write about councils using AI to clear **housing repair backlogs** instead of cutting staff.
think: I'm on the **right side** of this for a few years, because I already use the tools.
Fewer **junior hires** bothers me, because I was one of those juniors five years ago.
do: Set up **AI code review** and test-writing for the mobile team within a month.
Pitch an **AI pothole app** to councils so the company grows instead of shrinks.
Join the **union branch** and push for saved time to go into training.
feel: **Energised** but **guilty**, seeing a path for himself and others falling off.
S1.quote: I want the AI tools, and I want rules about who gets the time they save.
fieldNote: He feels **personally safe** for now, which fits uneasy despite thin savings.
His **guilt** about Rachel, the long-serving tester, is the most honest part.
He sees **automation and union rules** as one position, which he defends with Ines's example.

steps.text: Set up AI code review and test-writing for the mobile team
Run the team's AI training sessions and include Rachel
Join the tech workers' union branch and push training rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That changes everything, including my smug bit from the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency measures now: a basic income, a pause on mass layoffs, and public ownership of the big AI systems. I'd say it on every platform I've got. This stops being a tech story and becomes a story about who owns everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being good with the tools stops mattering. If AI can do any thinking work better than me, it can also use the AI better than me. My job is screens and logic, nothing hands-on, so I'd expect to be out within a year of 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the next two years I'd pay off my small credit card and build whatever savings I can, maybe two months. I'd try to get a council job in their digital team, because the public sector may move slower and protect people longer. If that fails, I'd help Dad run the shop properly while robots are still three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in a sharp way. Two years is barely enough time to change a phone contract, let alone a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You moved from smug to scared quickly. What changed in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slow version of AI I'm the guy with the tools; with AGI in two years I'm just another person whose skill got copied. Ines put it best: the difference is whether the tool needs you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the shop be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not safer, just slower. Someone still has to stack shelves and talk to Mrs Okafor about her grandson, at least until the robots come in 2031. It's three years of something, and that's more than my desk job offers.

say: I'd call for a **basic income**, a pause on mass layoffs and public ownership of AI.
I'd say this becomes a story about **who owns** everything, not a tech story.
think: Being good with the tools stops mattering if AI can **use AI better** than me.
My job is **screens and logic**, so I'd expect to be out within a year of 2028.
do: Pay off the credit card and build **two months** of savings before 2028.
Apply for a **council digital team** job, hoping the public sector moves slower.
Help Dad run the **corner shop** properly while robots are still years away.
feel: Sharp **fear**, because two years is barely enough to **change a career**.
S2.quote: In the slow version of AI I'm the guy with the tools; with AGI in two years I'm just another person whose skill got copied.
fieldNote: His **adaptability** stops protecting him here, and he says so plainly.
He looks to the **public sector** and his **dad's shop** as slower, hands-on fallbacks.
Ines's line about whether the **tool needs you** frames his whole view.

steps.text: Pay off the credit card and save two months' rent
Apply for a job in a council's in-house digital team
Campaign for a basic income and public ownership of AI
Work shifts in Dad's corner shop once the coding job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right, that's actually a plan's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something fair if we start now, not in 2030. I'd push for a public AI service that councils share, so the gains stay public. I'd be running workshops for other developers on what to do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get about three good years of being the AI person at work, then it thins out fast. I'd want to use those three years to build something that's mine. I'm still worried, but I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools to build small apps for charities on the side, charging a little, and grow that into a little co-op with two friends. I'd save hard while the salary lasts, aiming for four months. By 2030 I'd want the co-op paying half my rent, so the salary ending isn't a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but excited too. It's the feeling before a big exam you've actually studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the co-op face the same AGI in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know that. But a co-op that owns its AI tools keeps the savings, instead of a boss keeping them. And charities will want a human they trust to set things up for a while, even if the AI does the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ines think of the co-op idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says yes, as long as I don't quit my job before it pays. She's the careful one. She'd also want me home before nine, which is fair.

I'd push for a **public AI service** that councils share, so gains stay public.
think: I get about **three good years** as the AI person at work, then it thins out.
I'd want to build **something that's mine** in those three years.
do: Build small **charity apps** on the side with AI tools, charging a little.
Form a **co-op** with two friends and aim for half the rent by 2030.

feel: **Tense** but **excited**, like a big exam he's actually studied for.
S3.quote: A co-op that owns its AI tools keeps the savings, instead of a boss keeping them.
fieldNote: He turns his values into a **business shape**, the worker co-op.
He admits the co-op still faces AGI in 2031, a **clear-eyed** gap.
Ines acts as the **careful check** on his risk-taking.

steps.text: Build paid charity apps with AI tools in evenings
Set up a developer co-op with two friends by 2028
Save four months' rent while the salary lasts
Lobby councils to share a public AI service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, I like my odds better here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and if governments waste it, voters should remember. I'd push for AI to be treated like a public utility, the way water is. And I'd tell every junior I meet to learn people skills alongside code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty good about my own next five years. I'd be the person councils call to set these systems up. The worry is the second five years, and whether anyone who isn't already ahead gets a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two years getting really good with AI agents, the tools that build whole apps, and learn the council side of things, like contracts and data rules. I'd start the co-op slowly around year three. And I'd help Dad move his shop's stock and orders onto a simple app, because he's got ten years to make it work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a small worry at the edges. Ten years feels like enough time to land well if I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the second five years worry you. What's in them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's when the thinking work really goes, and then the robots three years after. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with kids, and running a co-op whose main product is me. I'd need to be on to the next thing by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ines change any plans with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for kids in a couple of years. Ines's job is mostly people, so it's slower to change. We'd just be stricter about saving, which we should be anyway.

I'd push for AI to be run like a **public utility**, the way water is.

The worry is the **second five years** and whether latecomers get a chance.

Start the **co-op** slowly around year three.

S4.quote: By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with kids, and running a co-op whose main product is me.
fieldNote: With ten years he sees his **own job safe** for now, so the mood is only uneasy.
He worries for **latecomers** more than for himself, a steady thread across scenarios.
Even his ambitious plan includes **Dad's shop**, showing family pulls on his choices.

steps.text: Learn AI agents that build whole apps over two years
Start the developer co-op slowly around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because all my plans need time, and that one gives me none. What would help is a basic income, plus public money to keep council digital teams going so people like me can do useful public work while things settle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who I'd want to own these systems. Everyone asks if AI will take my job, but nobody asks who should own the AI. If it's public, I'm much less scared.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if AI will take my job, but nobody asks who should own the AI.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** mobile developer building council apps like bin day reminders.
He lives with his partner Ines, a **social worker**, and sends money to his dad's shop.
He uses AI **every day** and feels on the right side of slow change.
His confidence breaks in **AGI by 2028**, where he expects to be out within a year.
His answers keep returning to **who owns AI**, and to a worker co-op as his plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because all his plans need time and that picture gives him none.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and public money for council **digital teams** during the change.
